transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-26 14:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Rivera (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Oryx - Head of MLOps), Priya Nair (Oryx - Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (Oryx - CTO)

Summary (auto): cost/unit deep dive, tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated, caching/batching levers and quantization options, plan to benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna focus today on cost economics and how batching and caching affect per-token. Marco will walk through the technicals, I'll cover pricing and next steps.
[00:18] Daniel: Yep thanks Sophie, we really want to understand unit costs vs latency. Our PQ is around 600 qps at peak for inference for our risk models, average prompt length is 120 tokens in, about 240 tokens out. Budget is roughly $25k/mo for model inference right now.
[00:36] Marco: cool, couple quick clarifying q's, is that 600 qps sustained or bursts?
[00:41] Daniel: it's bursty — sustained around 120 qps but spikes to 600 for short periods.
[00:48] Priya: also want to call out we need data residency in eu-west, and SOC2 plus SSO, we can talk security paperwork later.
[00:58] Sophie: noted. On pricing we have Hosted per-token + request overhead; Dedicated is a reserved capacity model with committed monthly GPU pools and effectively lower unit cost at scale. For Hosted typical per-token list rates are X cents for prompt and Y cents for completion but we'll send exact numbers, that's in the pricing sheet.
[01:20] Marco: technical levers — two big wins for unit cost are batching (increase GPU throughput) and KV/prefix caching for repeated context. For your workload with long shared context we can cache the prefix so incremental tokens are cheaper. Also quantization (8-bit/4-bit) can reduce inference cost on Dedicated.
[01:42] Liam: quick Q — when you say caching how much does it actually save?
[01:47] Marco: depends, example: if 60% of the prompt is identical across requests and we fully cache it, the per-request token compute drops ~60% for the prompt side; combined with batching improvements you can see 2-5x cost reduction depending on sequence lengths and hit rates. But caching improves tail latency slightly because less generation work, though cache misses still pay full cost.
[02:12] Daniel: ok that 2-5x number — what assumptions?
[02:16] Marco: assumptions: cache hit rate 50-70%, batching efficiency reaching effective token-per-GPU increases by ~30-100% depending on request arrival patterns, and quantization brings another 20-40% on Dedicated. We'll include a simple TCO calc that shows these knobs.
[02:36] Priya: we run multi-tenant models internally, how does your routing and isolation work for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[02:44] Sophie: Hosted is multi-tenant but with tenant isolation at the request level; Dedicated gives you reserved pools and network isolation, and Private gives full VPC with customer-managed control plane. For compliance you'd prefer Dedicated or Private.
[02:58] Liam: latency SLOs are critical for us — our risk scoring needs tail p95 under 200ms for short prompts. Does Dedicated help tail latency?
[03:06] Marco: yes Dedicated gives more consistent tail latency due to predictable capacity and less noisy neighbors; caching also reduces p95 for cached flows. For P95 200ms that is challenging for long outputs but for short prompts we can tune batching to prioritize low latency (smaller batch windows) at slightly higher unit cost.
[03:24] Daniel: so it's a tradeoff: prioritize latency and pay more, or batch for cost and accept higher tail. We need the math.
[03:30] Sophie: exactly. We'll share a TCO workbook that models per-token cost across dimensions: host vs dedicated, batch size/time window, cache hit rate, quantization level, and expected qps/sequence length distribution.
[03:45] Priya: on quantization — do you support mixed precision or do models need to be converted? Any risks to accuracy?
[03:52] Marco: we support 8-bit and some 4-bit quantized variants; accuracy delta is model-dependent — usually <2-3% on our evals for instruction style models, but you should run a quality regression on your prompts. We'll help with eval harness during the poc.
[04:10] Daniel: what's the typical ramp for Dedicated cost-wise? Like break-even point for moving from Hosted to Dedicated?
[04:16] Sophie: rough rule of thumb: if you're doing sustained high qps such that monthly token volume exceeds X million tokens, Dedicated often becomes cheaper because reserved GPU amortizes better. Exact number depends on your cache hit rate and batching efficiency; we'll compute break-even in the workbook.
[04:34] Liam: we care about predictable monthly spend — how flexible are committed pools? can we scale up/down?
[04:40] Sophie: Dedicated has autoscaling policies and burst capacity; contracts allow bandwidth for a baseline commit plus bursts — sales can model different commit levels to hit budget targets. Private is more capex-like but gives max control.
[04:52] Marco: from the infra side we can set QoS policies so certain routes get priority, and smaller batch windows for latency-sensitive endpoints while background ones get larger windows for cost-savings.
[05:06] Priya: for benchmarking, what do you need from us?
[05:09] Marco: ideally: 1) representative prompt set, 2) expected qps distribution (sustained vs peak), 3) target latency SLOs and accuracy pass/fail criteria. We'll run tests on Hosted and on a Dedicated test pool to show delta.
[05:22] Daniel: timeline — we want results in two weeks if possible.
[05:25] Sophie: we can do a light benchmark in ~1 week and a full TCO in two.
[05:30] Liam: security pack and SOC2 would be critical for procurement.
[05:33] Sophie: I'll send SOC2 and SSO docs with the pricing.
[05:36] Daniel: any gotchas around cost accounting? e.g., do you bill per-token generated including intermediates for tool-calls, or per final output tokens?
[05:43] Sophie: yes we bill per input and output tokens plus request metadata overhead; for streaming we meter tokens generated. For tool calling you may see extra tokens for tool prompts; we'll annotate those in the TCO.
[05:55] Marco: another note: prefix caching works best when prompts share context; if your prompts are mostly unique caching helps less. Also cold-start KV cache warmup can create transient load.
[06:08] Priya: ok we'll gather prompts and send them. On benchmarking environment do you need eu-west test endpoints?
[06:14] Marco: yes we can provision eu-west test Dedicated pool for the benchmark.
[06:18] Sophie: recap — Sophie send pricing/TCO + SOC2 and security pack; Marco run benchmark plan once Priya shares prompts and qps targets; Oryx to review and provide accuracy criteria.
[06:28] Daniel: cool sounds good.
[06:30] Liam: any competitors? we did some light evals with Apex Inference and Anthropic, but cost details were fuzzy.
[06:37] Sophie: noted. We'll include a short comparison table in the follow-up.
[06:41] Priya: thanks everyone.
[06:43] Sophie: thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark.
[06:48] End meeting
